Those disparities that used to be so regular were more about the poor AMD support not necessarily always technical inferiority. DX12 and Vulkan play to the new AMD line's technical advantages that they do possess. That's why it's disappointing to not see those APIs in so many of these reviews. They're better all around and Vulkan has showed impressive improvements in select games for each brand- and it's a huge deal since Vulkan could be the gateway to cutting Windows dependency for many more games. comments.text: So there are a few problems however. I'm going to point out the problems of ordering a GTX 1060 vs the RX 480. First off, GTX 1060 has a 192-bit memory interface whilst the RX 480 has a 256-bit, larger memory interfaces are always BETTER. Second off, 1060 has 6 GB of memory whilst RX 480 has 8 GB, therefore later in the future the RX 480 is more capable of handling VRAM intensive games or applications better due to having more VRAM. Third off, Aftermarket 480's have yet to be released, however there is rumors saying the RX 480 is better in game performance than an R9 Nano (Which personally was a great video card). Now of course there is also the factor that AMD cards are designed to better perform on DX12 vs DX11, so the only true way to decide which one is better is to run both on a DX12 game / application.

comments.text:
+Johnathan Bloch   Cut the bullshit lol.  If you knew anything about the specs you'd realize that makes no sense.  The 384 bit bus on the TITAN XP gives it a massive 480 GB/s bandwidth on the memory which is already just barely slower than HBM1 which runs at 512 GB/s.  And once you overclock the memory on the TITAN XP to ~11,000mhz effective (which is easily obtainable, most 1080's can hit even higher. My 1080 gets to 11,300mhz no problem) the bandwidth on the TITAN XP increases to 530 GB/s.  Even HBM2 only runs at ~700 GB/s. And at such high amounts, memory bandwidth has MAJOR diminishing returns; meaning that after a certain point more bandwidth becomes useless. It's basically getting similar to 8x vs 16x PCI-e lanes;  having your graphic card run at full 16x on the motherboard PCI slot gives it TWICE the bandwidth...but makes less than 1fps difference. This is because bandwidth after a certain point is useless as most Graphic Cards can't USE that much bandwidth. 

Think of bandwidth like the "size of the pipe" that water is flowing through; the graphic card is the pump pushing the water, and the memory itself is the water.  If you have one square inch of water flowing through a 1/2 inch wide pipe and then upgrade to a 1 inch pipe you will end up with much faster water delivery speeding things up; BUT, increasing the pump from 1 inch wide to 2 inch wide does basically nothing as there's only 1 square inch of water moving through it so the remaining inch of pipe gets mostly wasted not increasing speed at all. 

This diminishing returns combined with the fact that HBM2 isn't even able to be mass-produced for at least several months or so (early next year minimum, which is why Vega is delayed again and also why there's barely any Tesla P100's out there) and the fact that HBM2 is FAR more expensive, are the reasons why Nvidia didn't use it. Be glad they didn't; if they did you wouldn't see a TITAN XP and 1080 TI till at least middle of next year and it would be even MORE expensive than the card is now due to the higher cost of HBM2; and would literally provide nearly no extra performance over GDDR5X.

comments.text:
So many people complaining that they're testing DX11... DX12 performance varies so wildly from developer to developer and even title to title that it's almost impossible to do that. See also: Everybody bitching about TimeSpy's implementation.

Essentially, depending on what a developer chooses to do with DX12 rendering, it'll favour one architecture or another (async vs concurrency, etc). That's part of the territory when you go "close to metal" like Vulkan and DX12. In other words, unless you really want to know how one card plays one DX12 title vs another and not have any greater overall basis for comparison, then sure, DX12 benchmarks are for you. There just aren't enough DX12 titles to test for all scenarios yet, and not all DX12 titles are going to perform better than DX11 if the implementation sucks.

DX12 / Vulkan is not a magic bullet; It relies on game developers more than ever to make its advantages clear.

Retribution Hardware Unboxed uses early drivers for the new cards, of course there WERE minor issues. That doesn't mean NVidia and AMD are just going to throw up their hands and go 'oh well.' Fixes were released and implemented.
SLI and Crossfire isn't for most users, and those that do use it have either planned ahead or don't mind swapping out for more head room. Those looking to take it up usually wait to do a new build from the ground up anyways.
DirectX is only supported on Windows and Xbox natively, with artificial Linux support through app compatibility layers like Wine. Vulkan is supported on Windows, Linux, and Unix (Mac and PS4). DirectX isn't a indie developer of small developer favorite, they don't have the resources to recode a game to support one API for one platform, and another API for a different platform.
Vulkan has also been integrated into high profile engines, so using Vulkan for a good deal of games available only requires a few tweaks on Windows, it already happens on Linux.

I honestly feel like there's no such thing as an AMD fanboy when it comes to online graphics card reviews.  They're almost all biased towards Nvidia, which does make sense because Nvidia has put out some of the most badass cards ever but sometimes they overlook the technical side of things where almost every technology that Nvidia uses is restricted unlike AMD for whom most of their technologies are open for everyone to use.  Nvidia is anti-competitive in that way.  I'm talking mostly about AMD's TressFX and Nvidia's HairWorks, but also Mantle and CUDA/OpenCL.  AMD always uses the less restrictive technology.  It's just too easy for the GPU reviewers to just overlook the performance of AMD cards since the Nvidia cards will always appear to blow them out of the water, and not do the right thing by doing more benchmarks with certain setting switched off in order to level the playing field. 

There's a reason why the raw computing performance of AMD cards is actually much higher than the expected graphics performance when compared to an Nvidia card.

comments.text: 1060 will also get a perf boost from Vulkan.  The main performance increase due to Vulkan is from better utilization of CPU cores.  Doesn't have as much to do with the GPU. There are certain graphics rendering techniques used by AMD cards that Nvidia cards don't use and Vulkan was built to take advantage of all such features as it is not meant to favor any specific manufacturer or GPU design style.  It seems probable that DX11 slightly favored Nvidia in the past and for that reason those features hadn't been utilized to their full potential except in consoles where developers had access to hardware more similar to what Vulkan has to offer.

rx 480 got close to 980ti with vulcan on doom so if Pascal scales linearly 1060 won't catch rx 480 on that case sense 1060 would get too close to 1070 when the hardware isn't simply powerful enough. But it is what it is, 1060 might be simply bad with vulcan for all we know.

Now future proofing is another matter and AMD is simply better with dx12 and vulcan at the moment so if you are gonna keep that card around for next 4 years like most people tend to do, rx 480 will be better.
Now rx 480 does use more power, but the difference is not something to brag about. 
Both cards have clear advantages but if we are only talking about current performance in gaming well 1060 wins just and just slightly.

comments.text:
The reference 480 has a better PCB and better a better power delivery design than the GTX 1060 but a worse cooler and a more power hungry chip. Power-wise given how overkill the 480's board is the chip is likely never going to have any power issues, other than the PCI issue which had nothing to do with the board quality but rather how they divided the power delivery, the 6+1 phase was split into half from mobo, half from the power connector. All it took was to change the programming of the voltage controller to draw less from the mobo and the problem turned from an irrelevant issue to a nonexistent issue at all.

The RX 480 is fabbed on Global Foundries' 14nmLPP licensed from Samsung, a process which is well known to be worse than TSMC's 16nmFF+. (Apple A9 manufactured on Samsung's process consumes more power than A9 manufactured on TSMC's process)

Nvidia is making changes and pushing tech forward?

AMD's GCN architecure has more "meat", metaphorically speaking.
 
AMD has hardware schedulers, (nVidia does the task scheduling in software, i.e on the CPU) which take up space on the chip and drives up power. Many RX 480 reviews that tested total system power out of the wall recorded 20-30w less than the GTX 970, despite the card itself drawing as much power as the 970, this is due to the hardware scheduling, which takes a large load off of the CPU, which drives down power.

AMD also has Async Compute Engines, which are for Async Compute, obviously, they also take die space and power. Did you know AMD invented Async Compute? Async Compute is a key feature of DX12 and Vulkan. DX12 and Vulkan are heavily based on Mantle, an API that AMD first developed. DX12 especially is on the road to mainstream adoption, with many games like Battlefield 1, Deus Ex, Watch Dogs 2, and Civ VI on the way. By now we all know the benefits of DX12 and Async Compute, AMD sees some phenomenal gains with DX12 and Vulkan. 

(And before anyone claims cripple ware or anything. Vulkan is owned by the Khronos Group, a group Nvidia is part of, and it's president is a Nvidia employee. Nvidia has also been promoting DX12 heavily. AMD and Nvidia have also done a joint presentation about DX12 at GDC)

On a game like DOOM in Vulkan, where both Nvidia and AMD GPUs are pushed to their limit, the AMD GPUs come out ahead. Keep in mind id Software worked with both Nvidia and AMD. In fact they demonstrated DOOM with Vulkan on Nvidia hardware before AMD did.

This also in no way precludes other devs from making meh DX12/Vulkan games. Rise of the Tomb Raider and Hitman favor Nvidia and AMD in that order and are known to be somewhat buggy.

Creating a paradigm shift in game development (one that shows the true power of their hardware) is definitely a big quantifiable change.

Nvidia has also been removing DP units from their SM's ever since Kepler, which results in completely nerfed and destroyed double precision performance, in exchange for lower power consumption. (The vast majority of games shaders do not need fp64 calculations)

AMD on the other hand has always been able to fuse two single precision units to do double precision, which is something Nvidia has never been able to do and makes GCN a far more flexible architecture for compute. 

Speaking of compute, AMD also has consistently higher peak TFLOPS performance than Nvidia, ever since the first iteration of GCN. AMD has also released cards that have always had more VRAM and more bandwith, which is also very useful for compute and professional applications.

Speaking of memory, AMD has also invented HBM, a technology that both reduces power and increases bandwidth. A technology that Nvidia uses for their 15B transistor monster GP100.

I'm not an Nvidia hater. In fact I'm an Nvidia owner. They've made some great cards . They've introduced some game changing technologies in GPUs such as delta color compression and with Pascal simultaneous multiprojection, but I am done with people sucking their dick.
